title: Response-Time Analysis for Non-Preemptive Global Scheduling with FIFO Spin Locks

extraction.paper_name: Response-Time Analysis for Non-Preemptive Global Scheduling with FIFO Spin Locks
extraction.paper_description: This paper presents a novel response-time analysis for non-preemptive global job-level fixed-priority (JLFP) scheduling policies on multicore platforms, specifically considering shared resources protected by FIFO spin locks. The analysis implicitly explores all possible execution scenarios using a schedule-abstraction graph (SAG) with a new system-state abstraction, providing worst-case response time (WCRT) bounds for jobs subject to release jitter and execution-time uncertainties.

formal_description.statement: A job J_i is defined by its release time interval, deadline, priority, and sequence of segments: J_i = ([r_min_i, r_max_i], d_i, p_i, J_i_1, ..., J_i_ni)

variables.r_min_i: Earliest release time of job J_i
variables.r_max_i: Latest release time of job J_i
variables.n_i: Total number of segments in job J_i

assumptions: Timing parameters are discrete (integer multiples of a clock tick)
Jobs execute sequentially on one core with run-to-completion semantics
Segments inherit the job's priority
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fundamental properties of a job in the system model.

informal_sketch.intuition: Each piece of work (job) has a window when it can arrive, a deadline by which it must finish, a priority, and is broken down into smaller, sequential parts (segments).
steps: A job J_i is characterized by:
- Its earliest possible release time (r_min_i)
- Its latest possible release time (r_max_i)
- Its absolute deadline (d_i)
- Its fixed priority (p_i)
- A sequence of job segments (J_i_1 to J_i_ni) that must execute in order.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class Job:
    def __init__(self, id, r_min, r_max, deadline, priority, segments):
        self.id = id
        self.r_min = r_min
        self.r_max = r_max
        self.deadline = deadline
        self.priority = priority
        self.segments = segments # List of JobSegment objects
        self.n_segments = len(segments)
key_insights: Jobs have release jitter (r_min_i to r_max_i).
Jobs are non-preemptive once started.
Jobs are composed of sequential segments.

formal_description.statement:
A job segment J_i_j is defined by its execution time interval, requested resources, and critical section length interval: J_i_j = ([C_min_i_j, C_max_i_j], eta_i_j, [L_min_i_j, L_max_i_j]).
Constraint: L_min_i_j <= C_min_i_j and L_max_i_j <= C_max_i_j.

variables.C_min_i_j: Best-case execution time (BCET) of segment J_i_j
variables.C_max_i_j: Worst-case execution time (WCET) of segment J_i_j
variables.eta_i_j: Set of resources requested by segment J_i_j
variables.L_min_i_j: Minimum length of critical section for resource in eta_i_j
variables.L_max_i_j: Maximum length of critical section for resource in eta_i_j

assumptions: Each segment J_i_j can access at most one resource protected by a lock (|eta_i_j| is 0 or 1).
The critical section of a segment is located at the beginning of the segment.
The segment must first be granted the lock protecting the shared resource in eta_i_j (if any) to start executing.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the properties of individual job segments, including execution variability and resource access.

informal_sketch.intuition: Each part of a job (segment) has a variable execution time and might need to access a shared resource, which involves a critical section of variable length.
steps: A segment J_i_j is characterized by:
- Its best-case (C_min_i_j) and worst-case (C_max_i_j) execution times.
- The set of shared resources it needs (eta_i_j).
- The minimum (L_min_i_j) and maximum (L_max_i_j) duration of its critical section.
The critical section length must be less than or equal to the segment's execution time.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class JobSegment:
    def __init__(self, id, C_min, C_max, resources, L_min, L_max):
        self.id = id
        self.C_min = C_min
        self.C_max = C_max
        self.resources = resources # Set of resource IDs
        self.L_min = L_min
        self.L_max = L_max
        assert L_min <= C_min and L_max <= C_max
key_insights: Execution times and critical section lengths are uncertain (intervals).
Resource access is modeled explicitly, with critical sections at the start of segments.
FIFO spin locks are used for resource protection.

formal_description.statement:
An execution scenario gamma is a mapping of jobs to release times, segment execution times, and critical-section lengths such that:
∀J_i ∈ J, r_i ∈ [r_min_i, r_max_i]
∀j, 1 ≤ j ≤ n_i, C_i_j ∈ [C_min_i_j, C_max_i_j]
∀j, 1 ≤ j ≤ n_i, L_i_j ∈ [L_min_i_j, L_max_i_j]

variables.J: The finite set of non-preemptive jobs being analyzed
variables.J_i: A specific job in the set J
variables.r_i: Actual release time of job J_i in scenario gamma
variables.r_min_i: Earliest release time of job J_i
variables.r_max_i: Latest release time of job J_i
variables.n_i: Total number of segments in job J_i
variables.C_i_j: Actual execution time of segment J_i_j in scenario gamma
variables.C_min_i_j: Best-case execution time of segment J_i_j
variables.C_max_i_j: Worst-case execution time of segment J_i_j
variables.L_i_j: Actual critical-section length of segment J_i_j in scenario gamma
variables.L_min_i_j: Minimum critical-section length of segment J_i_j
variables.L_max_i_j: Maximum critical-section length of segment J_i_j

assumptions: The job set J is defined for an observation window that is representative of the system workload.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific, valid instantiation of all uncertain timing parameters (release times, execution times, critical section lengths) within their specified intervals.

informal_sketch.intuition: An 'execution scenario' is one specific way the system could behave, where all uncertain timings (when jobs arrive, how long segments run, how long critical sections last) are chosen within their allowed ranges.
steps: To define an execution scenario (gamma):
1. For each job J_i in the job set J, pick an actual release time (r_i) such that r_min_i <= r_i <= r_max_i.
2. For each segment J_i_j of every job J_i, pick an actual execution time (C_i_j) such that C_min_i_j <= C_i_j <= C_max_i_j.
3. For each segment J_i_j, pick an actual critical-section length (L_i_j) such that L_min_i_j <= L_i_j <= L_max_i_j.
key_insights: This definition captures all sources of timing uncertainty in the system.
Schedulability requires that *no* such scenario leads to a deadline miss.

formal_description.statement: For any two paths P and Q, if both P and Q start at v_1 and end in v_p, then J_P = J_Q.

variables.P: A path in the Schedule-Abstraction Graph (SAG)
variables.v_1: The initial state of the system at time zero
variables.v_p: A specific abstract system state (vertex) in the SAG
variables.J_P: The set of job segments that are labels on the edges of path P
variables.J_Q: The set of job segments that are labels on the edges of path Q

assumptions: The graph G = (V, E) is a directed acyclic graph (SAG).
Edges are labeled with job segments J_i_j, indicating execution.
formal_description.conclusion: Any two paths leading to the same abstract state v_p must have scheduled the exact same set of job segments, regardless of the order.

informal_sketch.intuition: If you reach the same 'abstract state' in our analysis, it means you've completed the same set of tasks, even if the order in which you completed them was different. The abstract state summarizes the *effect* of these completed tasks.
steps: Consider a Schedule-Abstraction Graph (SAG) where nodes are system states and edges are scheduling decisions (executing a job segment).

If two different sequences of scheduling decisions (paths P and Q) both start from the initial state (v_1) and lead to the *same* final abstract state (v_p), then the *collection* of job segments executed along path P must be identical to the collection of job segments executed along path Q.
The order of execution might differ, but the set of completed segments is the same.
key_insights: This property is crucial for the soundness of state merging in the SAG.
It allows the analysis to abstract away the exact order of execution for segments that have already completed, as long as the *set* of completed segments is the same.
This helps manage state-space explosion by allowing 'similar' states to be merged.

formal_description.statement: For each job J_i ∈ C(v_p), we record the interval [Cl_min_i(v_p), Cl_max_i(v_p)], where Cl_min_i(v_p) and Cl_max_i(v_p) indicate when the core claimed by job J_i becomes possibly and certainly available to execute the next segment of J_i, respectively.

variables.v_p: An abstract system state (vertex) in the SAG
variables.J_i: A job that has claimed a core
variables.C(v_p): The set of jobs that have claimed a core in state v_p
variables.Cl_min_i(v_p): Earliest time the core claimed by J_i is available for its next segment in state v_p
variables.Cl_max_i(v_p): Latest time the core claimed by J_i is available for its next segment in state v_p

assumptions: A job 'claims' a core once its first segment starts execution and 'releases' it upon completion of its last segment.
Jobs execute non-preemptively.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the time interval during which a core, currently dedicated to an ongoing job, will become free for that job's *next* segment.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a job has started but not finished, it 'owns' a core. This definition tracks when that core will be ready for the *next* part of that same job, considering execution time uncertainties.
steps: For any job J_i that has started executing but not yet completed all its segments (i.e., it 'claims' a core):
1. Cl_min_i(v_p) is the earliest possible time that the core J_i is using will be ready for J_i's next segment.
2. Cl_max_i(v_p) is the latest possible time that the core J_i is using will be ready for J_i's next segment.
This interval reflects the uncertainty in the finish time of J_i's currently executing segment.
key_insights: Crucial for tracking the progress of multi-segment jobs.
Reflects the non-preemptive nature: a core is dedicated to a job until its current segment finishes.

formal_description.statement: We record m - |C(v_p)| intervals A_x(v_p) = [A_min_x(v_p), A_max_x(v_p)] such that 1 ≤ x ≤ m - |C(v_p)|, which indicate when one, two, three, ..., m - |C(v_p)| free cores (i.e., those that are not already claimed by executing jobs) become possibly and certainly available to execute ready jobs.

variables.v_p: An abstract system state (vertex) in the SAG
variables.m: Number of identical cores on the multicore platform
variables.C(v_p): The set of jobs that have claimed a core in state v_p
variables.A_x(v_p): The availability interval for the x-th free core in state v_p
variables.A_min_x(v_p): Earliest time the x-th free core is available in state v_p
variables.A_max_x(v_p): Latest time the x-th free core is available in state v_p

assumptions: Cores are identical.
A core is 'free' if no job has claimed it (i.e., no job has started its first segment on it and not yet finished its last segment).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the time intervals during which available cores (not currently claimed by ongoing jobs) become free for new jobs to start.

informal_sketch.intuition: This tracks when idle processors become available for new jobs. Since there can be multiple idle processors, it tracks the availability of the 1st, 2nd, ..., (m - claimed_cores)th available processor.
steps: For a system with 'm' cores, if '|C(v_p)|' cores are currently claimed by ongoing jobs, then 'm - |C(v_p)|' cores are free.
For each of these free cores (indexed x from 1 to m - |C(v_p)|):
1. A_min_x(v_p) is the earliest possible time the x-th free core becomes available.
2. A_max_x(v_p) is the latest possible time the x-th free core becomes available.
These intervals are typically sorted, so A_min_1(v_p) refers to the earliest available free core, A_min_2(v_p) to the second earliest, and so on.
key_insights: Models the availability of multiple processors for new job dispatches.
The intervals reflect the uncertainty in when jobs currently using cores will finish and release them.
Crucial for work-conserving schedulers that dispatch jobs to any available core.

formal_description.statement:
For each shared resource x ∈ L, a state records the interval [SR_min_x(v_p), SR_max_x(v_p)], where SR_min_x(v_p) and SR_max_x(v_p) denote the times at which x become possibly and certainly available again, respectively.
For ease of reference, we also introduce SR_min_i_j(v_p) and SR_max_i_j(v_p) to refer to the availability interval of the resource accessed by segment J_i_j (if any). Hence, if J_i_j accesses a shared resource (i.e., ∃ x ∈ eta_i_j), then SR_min_i_j(v_p) and SR_max_i_j(v_p) are the earliest and latest availability time SR_min_x(v_p) and SR_max_x(v_p) of the resource x accessed by J_i_j. If J_i_j does not access a resource, then SR_min_i_j(v_p) = SR_max_i_j(v_p) = 0.

variables.v_p: An abstract system state (vertex) in the SAG
variables.L: The set of shared resources protected by locks
variables.SR_min_x(v_p): Earliest time resource x is available in state v_p
variables.SR_max_x(v_p): Latest time resource x is available in state v_p
variables.eta_i_j: Set of resources requested by segment J_i_j
variables.SR_min_i_j(v_p): Earliest time the resource requested by J_i_j is available
variables.SR_max_i_j(v_p): Latest time the resource requested by J_i_j is available

assumptions: Resources are protected by FIFO spin locks.
A resource is 'available' if no job is currently accessing it.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the time interval during which a shared resource becomes available for new requests, considering current usage and critical section uncertainties.

informal_sketch.intuition: This tracks when shared resources (like data structures protected by locks) become free. If a resource is currently in use, this tells us the earliest and latest times it might be released.
steps: For each shared resource 'x':
1. SR_min_x(v_p) is the earliest possible time resource 'x' becomes available.
2. SR_max_x(v_p) is the latest possible time resource 'x' becomes available.
If a segment J_i_j needs a resource, SR_min_i_j(v_p) and SR_max_i_j(v_p) refer to the availability of that specific resource.
If J_i_j doesn't need a resource, its resource availability interval is [0, 0] (meaning it's always available from time 0).
key_insights: Models contention for shared data.
FIFO spin locks imply that requests are served in arrival order, which is critical for blocking analysis.
Uncertainty in critical section lengths directly impacts resource availability intervals.

results.identifier: Formula (1): Set of Potentially Ready Segments (R_P)

formal_description.statement: R_P = {J_i_j | J_i_j ∉ J_P ∧ (j = 1 ∨ J_i_j-1 ∈ J_P)}

variables.R_P: The set of potentially ready job segments for a given path P
variables.J_P: The set of job segments that have already started executing on path P
variables.j: The index of the segment within its job J_i
variables.J_i_j-1: The segment immediately preceding J_i_j within the same job J_i

assumptions: A path P represents a sequence of scheduling decisions.
Segments within a job execute sequentially.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the set of job segments that are candidates to be scheduled next, meaning they haven't started yet, and their preceding segments (if any) have already started.

informal_sketch.intuition: A job segment is 'potentially ready' if it hasn't started executing yet, and either it's the very first segment of its job, or the segment right before it in the same job has already begun (and might have finished).
steps: To find the set R_P of potentially ready segments for a given path P (which represents a partial schedule):
1. Iterate through all job segments J_i_j in the system.
2. Include J_i_j in R_P if it meets two conditions:
a. J_i_j has NOT yet started executing on path P (i.e., J_i_j is not in J_P).
b. Either J_i_j is the first segment of its job (j = 1), OR its immediate predecessor segment (J_i_j-1) *has* already started executing on path P (i.e., J_i_j-1 is in J_P).
key_insights: This set identifies all segments that are logically ready to proceed, based on their internal job dependencies.
It's a prerequisite for a segment to be considered for scheduling by the scheduler.

results.identifier: Lemma 1: Earliest Start Time Lower Bound

formal_description.statement: Segment J_i_j ∈ R_P cannot start executing (as a successor of state v_p) before EST_i_j(v_p).

variables.R_P: The set of potentially ready job segments
variables.EST_i_j(v_p): The earliest start time of segment J_i_j in state v_p

assumptions: J_i_j is in the set of potentially ready segments R_P.
formal_description.conclusion: EST_i_j(v_p) provides a safe lower bound on when J_i_j can begin execution.

informal_sketch.intuition: A segment can't start until all its prerequisites are met: it's released, its previous segments are done, a core is free, and any requested shared resources are available. EST_i_j(v_p) calculates the earliest possible moment all these conditions could be true.
steps: The proof for this lemma (and the definition of EST_i_j(v_p) in Formula (2)) considers three cases:
1. If J_i_j is the first segment of its job (j=1) and all 'm' cores are already claimed: It cannot start, so EST_i_j(v_p) is infinity.

2. If J_i_j is the first segment (j=1) and there's at least one free core: It needs to be released (r_min_i), a free core must be available (A_min_1(v_p)), and its resource (if any) must be available (SR_min_i_j(v_p)). It starts no earlier than the maximum of these times.

3. If J_i_j is not the first segment (j>1): It needs its claimed core to be available (Cl_min_i(v_p)) and its resource (if any) to be available (SR_min_i_j(v_p)). It starts no earlier than the maximum of these times.
key_insights: EST_i_j(v_p) is a lower bound, meaning the segment *cannot* start before this time in *any* scenario.
It accounts for release jitter, core availability, and shared resource availability.
The non-preemptive nature means a job claims a core until its segments complete.

dependencies: Formula (1): Set of Potentially Ready Segments (R_P)

formal_description.statement:
EST_i_j(v_p) = ⎧ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎩ ∞ if j = 1 ∧ |C(v_p)| = m
max{r_min_i, A_min_1(v_p), SR_min_i_j(v_p)} if j = 1 ∧ |C(v_p)| < m
max{Cl_min_i(v_p), SR_min_i_j(v_p)} if j > 1

variables.EST_i_j(v_p): Earliest start time of segment J_i_j in state v_p
variables.j: Index of the segment within its job J_i
variables.C(v_p): Set of jobs that have claimed a core in state v_p
variables.r_min_i: Earliest release time of job J_i
variables.A_min_1(v_p): Earliest time the first free core is available in state v_p
variables.SR_min_i_j(v_p): Earliest time the resource requested by J_i_j is available
variables.Cl_min_i(v_p): Earliest time the core claimed by J_i is available for its next segment

assumptions: J_i_j is in R_P.
A_min_1(v_p) refers to the earliest available free core.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides the formal calculation for the earliest start time of a job segment, based on its type (first or subsequent segment) and system resource availability.

informal_sketch.intuition: This formula precisely defines the earliest a segment can start. It's either impossible (infinity), or the latest of when the job is released, a core is free, and its resource is free (for first segments), or the latest of when its dedicated core is free and its resource is free (for subsequent segments).
steps: 1. **If J_i_j is the first segment (j=1) AND all 'm' cores are currently claimed:** The segment cannot start because there are no free cores. So, EST_i_j(v_p) is set to infinity.

2. **If J_i_j is the first segment (j=1) AND there is at least one free core (|C(v_p)| < m):** The segment can start only after its job J_i is released (r_min_i), the earliest free core becomes available (A_min_1(v_p)), and any shared resource it needs becomes available (SR_min_i_j(v_p)). EST_i_j(v_p) is the maximum of these three times.

3. **If J_i_j is not the first segment (j>1):** The segment is part of an ongoing job that has already claimed a core. It can start only after its dedicated core becomes available (Cl_min_i(v_p)) and any shared resource it needs becomes available (SR_min_i_j(v_p)). EST_i_j(v_p) is the maximum of these two times.
key_insights: This formula is the core of determining when a segment can *possibly* begin.
It directly incorporates the system state (core and resource availability) and job parameters (release times, segment type).
The 'infinity' case correctly models scenarios where a segment cannot start due to lack of resources.

results.identifier: Lemma 8: Earliest Resource Request Time Lower Bound

formal_description.statement: Segment J_i_j ∈ R_P cannot request a shared resource in v_p earlier than ERT_i_j(v_p).

variables.R_P: The set of potentially ready job segments
variables.ERT_i_j(v_p): The earliest resource request time of segment J_i_j in state v_p

assumptions: J_i_j is in the set of potentially ready segments R_P.
A segment requests its resource as soon as it starts executing.
formal_description.conclusion: ERT_i_j(v_p) provides a safe lower bound on when J_i_j can make its resource request.

informal_sketch.intuition: A segment can't request a resource until its job is released and it has a core to run on. ERT_i_j(v_p) calculates the earliest possible moment these conditions are met, allowing it to make the request.
steps: The proof for this lemma (and the definition of ERT_i_j(v_p) in Formula (9)) considers two cases:

1. If J_i_j is the first segment of its job (j=1): It cannot request a resource before its job is released (r_min_i) and a core becomes available for it to start (A_min_1(v_p)). The earliest request time is the maximum of these.

2. If J_i_j is not the first segment (j>1): It is part of an ongoing job. It requests the resource as soon as its preceding segment completes, which is lower-bounded by the availability of its claimed core (Cl_min_i(v_p)).
key_insights: This bound is crucial for analyzing FIFO spin locks, as the order of resource requests determines the order of access.
It separates the resource request time from the resource *availability* time, which is important for blocking analysis.

dependencies: Formula (1): Set of Potentially Ready Segments (R_P)

formal_description.statement:
ERT_i_j(v_p) = ⎧ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎩ max{r_min_i, A_min_1(v_p)} if j = 1
Cl_min_i(v_p) if j > 1

variables.ERT_i_j(v_p): Earliest resource request time of segment J_i_j in state v_p
variables.j: Index of the segment within its job J_i
variables.r_min_i: Earliest release time of job J_i
variables.A_min_1(v_p): Earliest time the first free core is available in state v_p
variables.Cl_min_i(v_p): Earliest time the core claimed by J_i is available for its next segment

assumptions: J_i_j is in R_P.
A segment requests its resource as soon as it starts executing.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides the formal calculation for the earliest time a job segment can request its shared resource.

informal_sketch.intuition: This formula defines the earliest moment a segment can 'ask' for a resource. For a first segment, it's when the job is released and a core is free. For subsequent segments, it's when its dedicated core is free from the previous segment.
steps: 1. **If J_i_j is the first segment (j=1):** It can request a resource only after its job J_i is released (r_min_i) and a core becomes available for it to start (A_min_1(v_p)). ERT_i_j(v_p) is the maximum of these two times.

2. **If J_i_j is not the first segment (j>1):** It is part of an ongoing job. It requests the resource as soon as its preceding segment completes, which is lower-bounded by the availability of its claimed core (Cl_min_i(v_p)). So, ERT_i_j(v_p) is Cl_min_i(v_p).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_ERT_formula(job_id, segment_idx, state_p):
    if segment_idx == 1: # First segment
        r_min_i = get_job_r_min(job_id)
        A_min_1_vp = state_p.free_cores_availability[0][0] if state_p.free_cores_availability else float('inf')
        return max(r_min_i, A_min_1_vp)
    else: # Not the first segment
        Cl_min_i_vp = state_p.claimed_cores_availability[job_id][0]
        return Cl_min_i_vp
key_insights: This formula is critical for determining the queueing order for FIFO spin locks.
It highlights the distinction between a job being ready to execute (and thus request a resource) and the resource actually being available.

results.identifier: Lemma 2: Upper Bound on Certain Start Time (tw_y_z)

formal_description.statement: An upper bound on the time at which a segment J_y_z can certainly start executing (as a successor of state v_p) is given by tw_y_z.

variables.tw_y_z: Upper bound on the time J_y_z can certainly start executing

assumptions: J_y_z is in R_P (potentially ready).
formal_description.conclusion: tw_y_z provides a safe upper bound, meaning J_y_z will certainly have started by this time if it is the next segment to be scheduled.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma defines the latest moment a segment *must* have started, assuming it's the next one to be scheduled. It's based on the latest possible release time, latest core availability, and latest resource availability.
steps: The proof for this lemma (and the definition of tw_y_z in Formula (3)) considers three cases:
1. If J_y_z is the first segment (z=1) and all 'm' cores are claimed: It cannot start, so tw_y_z is infinity.

2. If J_y_z is the first segment (z=1) and there's at least one free core: It needs to be certainly released (r_max_y), a free core must be certainly available (A_max_1(v_p)), and its resource (if any) must be certainly available (SR_max_y_z(v_p)). It certainly starts by the maximum of these times.

3. If J_y_z is not the first segment (z>1): It needs its claimed core to be certainly available (Cl_max_y(v_p)) and its resource (if any) to be certainly available (SR_max_y_z(v_p)). It certainly starts by the maximum of these times.
key_insights: tw_y_z is an upper bound, meaning the segment *will* have started by this time in *any* scenario if it's the next one to be scheduled.
It uses the 'max' of latest times because all conditions must be met for the segment to start.
This is crucial for determining the latest possible point a work-conserving scheduler *must* dispatch a job.

formal_description.statement:

def calculate_LRT_formula(job_id, segment_idx, state_p):

    if segment_idx == 1: # First segment
        r_max_y = get_job_r_max(job_id)
        A_max_1_vp = state_p.free_cores_availability[0][1] if state_p.free_cores_availability else float('inf')
        return max(r_max_y, A_max_1_vp)
    else: # Not the first segment
        Cl_max_y_vp = state_p.claimed_cores_availability[job_id][1]
        return Cl_max_y_vp

def is_eligible_theorem_1(segment_ij, job_i, state_p, all_jobs, m):
    EST_val = calculate_EST_formula(job_i.id, segment_ij.id, state_p, m)
    LST_val = calculate_LST_formula(calculate_t_wc_formula(get_potentially_ready_segments(all_jobs, state_p.started_segments), state_p, m), 
                                    calculate_t_high_formula(segment_ij, job_i, get_potentially_ready_segments(all_jobs, state_p.started_segments), state_p))

    # Condition 1 & 2 (from Lemma 7)
    if not (EST_val < float('inf') and EST_val <= LST_val):
        return False

    # Condition 3 (FIFO resource ordering)
    if segment_ij.resources: # If J_i_j requests a resource
        resource_id_ij = list(segment_ij.resources)[0]
        ERT_ij_vp = calculate_ERT_formula(job_i.id, segment_ij.id, state_p)

        R_P = get_potentially_ready_segments(all_jobs, state_p.started_segments)
        for job_y_id, segment_y_idx in R_P:
            segment_yz = get_segment_object(job_y_id, segment_y_idx)
            if segment_yz.resources and list(segment_yz.resources)[0] == resource_id_ij: # If J_y_z requests the same resource
                if (job_y_id, segment_y_idx) != (job_i.id, segment_ij.id): # Exclude J_i_j itself
                    LRT_yz_vp = calculate_LRT_formula(job_y_id, segment_y_idx, state_p)
                    if ERT_ij_vp > LRT_yz_vp:
                        return False # J_y_z certainly requested resource earlier
    return True

formal_description.conclusion: Provides the rules for updating the sets of possible (PA) and certain (CA) availability times for free cores in the new system state v_q, considering the type of segment J_i_j (first, intermediate, or last) and its impact on core availability.

informal_sketch.intuition: When a segment starts, it changes which cores are free and when. This lemma defines how to calculate the new earliest and latest availability times for all free cores, considering if the segment takes a free core, keeps a claimed core, or releases a claimed core.
steps: 1. **General Rule (Fact 1):** No core can become available before EST_i_j, as the system is busy until then. So, all new availability times are at least EST_i_j.
2. **Case: J_i_j is the first segment (j=1):**
a. It takes one free core. The other free cores' availability is updated by max(EST_i_j, A_min_x/A_max_x) for x from 2 to m-|C(v_p)| (Fact 3).
b. If J_i_j is also the *last* segment (j=n_i), the core it just used becomes free upon its completion. So, EFT_i_ni and LFT_i_ni are added to PA and CA, respectively (Fact 5).
3. **Case: J_i_j is an intermediate segment (1 < j < n_i):**
a. It uses an already claimed core, so the number of free cores doesn't change. All free cores' availability is updated by max(EST_i_j, A_min_x/A_max_x) for x from 1 to m-|C(v_p)| (Fact 4).
4. **Case: J_i_j is the last segment (j=n_i) but not the first (j>1):**

a. It uses an already claimed core, but then releases it. The number of free cores increases by one. The existing free cores' availability is updated by max(EST_i_j, A_min_x/A_max_x) for x from 1 to m-|C(v_p)| (Fact 2).
b. The core J_i_j just released becomes free, so EFT_i_ni and LFT_i_ni are added to PA and CA, respectively (Fact 5).

def update_free_cores_lemma_11(state_p, job_i, segment_ij, EST_ij_val, EFT_ij_val, LFT_ij_val, m):
    PA = []
    CA = []
    num_claimed_cores_vp = len(state_p.claimed_cores_availability)

    if segment_ij.is_first_segment(): # j == 1
        # J_i_j takes one free core, so start from the second free core's availability
        for x in range(1, m - num_claimed_cores_vp):
            PA.append(max(EST_ij_val, state_p.free_cores_availability[x][0]))
            CA.append(max(EST_ij_val, state_p.free_cores_availability[x][1]))
        if segment_ij.is_last_segment(): # j == n_i
            # The core J_i_j used becomes free
            PA.append(EFT_ij_val)
            CA.append(LFT_ij_val)
    else: # j > 1 (not the first segment)
        # J_i_j uses an already claimed core, so all existing free cores remain free
        for x in range(m - num_claimed_cores_vp):
            PA.append(max(EST_ij_val, state_p.free_cores_availability[x][0]))
            CA.append(max(EST_ij_val, state_p.free_cores_availability[x][1]))
        if segment_ij.is_last_segment(): # j == n_i
            # The core J_i_j used becomes free
            PA.append(EFT_ij_val)
            CA.append(LFT_ij_val)
    
    # Sort PA and CA to get A_x intervals for the new state
    PA.sort()
    CA.sort()
    new_free_cores_availability = []
    for i in range(len(PA)):
        new_free_cores_availability.append([PA[i], CA[i]])
    return new_free_cores_availability

It accounts for the non-preemptive nature and the fact that jobs can claim and release cores.
The distinction between first/intermediate/last segments is vital for correctly updating the set of free cores.
The 'max(EST_i_j, ...)' ensures that no core appears available before the system has progressed to EST_i_j.
